title: How blue-state Republicans can be relevant again
gist: Yglesias endorses a new bipartisan Senate permitting-reform deal (transmission, tech-neutral permitting, data centers paying for grid upgrades) and urges Congress to pass it now rather than wait. In the mailbag he argues blue-state Republicans could be competitive by copying the federal GOP formula of business-friendly economics plus selective culture war, but are hobbled by Trump loyalty, a preference for complaining over winning, and NIMBY opposition to zoning reform; he also treats AI-enabled hacking as a 'normal technology' problem solvable via common-law liability and AI-enabled cybersecurity.

insights.claim: A new bipartisan Senate permitting reform package is very strong, combining easier electricity transmission, tech-neutral provisions improving speed and certainty for energy project permitting, and data-center provisions so new large loads pay the cost of grid upgrades.
insights.so_what: If passed, faster transmission and permitting would benefit grid developers, renewables, geothermal and utilities, while large-load cost allocation could raise data-center interconnection costs for hyperscalers.
insights.quote: some good ideas around data centers to make sure new large loads pay the cost of grid upgrades
insights.locator: Before we get to the questions
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich negotiated many wins for electrification, renewables and geothermal in the permitting bill, which also contains concessions to the fossil fuel industry.
insights.so_what: A balanced package with both clean-energy and fossil concessions improves odds of bipartisan passage and broad energy-sector benefit.
insights.quote: Whitehouse and Senator Martin Heinrich negotiated a ton of wins for electrification and renewables and geothermal in this bill
insights.locator: If you’re a person who cannot countenance
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: The main risk to the permitting bill is opponents punting it to the next Congress by claiming a better deal is coming next spring, wasting another year or two instead of letting the next Democratic administration hit the ground running on renewables build-out.
insights.so_what: Watch for delay tactics in the lame-duck window; failure would push permitting reform and transmission build-out timelines out by years.
insights.quote: The risk is that people who at heart don’t want a deal kick it into the next Congress
insights.locator: Now, Congress should pass the bill!
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Any permitting bill Donald Trump could sign in 2027-2028, or that could pass even a filibuster-free Senate whose Democratic majority depends on Texas and Alaska, will necessarily include concessions to fossil fuels, so a better climate-only deal is unrealistic.
insights.so_what: Structural Senate math means fossil-fuel concessions are a durable feature of any energy legislation.
insights.locator: If you’re a person who cannot countenance
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Yglesias says he misjudged Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, whose climate-messaging push seemed misguided but was coupled with a determination to negotiate substantive legislation.
insights.so_what: Signals a pro-deal coalition forming between climate hawks and abundance-minded centrists.
insights.quote: I also need to say that I misjudged Senator Sheldon Whitehouse
insights.locator: I also need to say
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: The federal Republican formula is to deploy culture-war issues for maximal electoral benefit and then pursue business-friendly economic policy, dropping issues like opposition to gay marriage once they become bad politics (run hard on in 2004, dropped by 2016).
insights.so_what: Implies GOP cultural positions are electorally instrumental and adjustable, while pro-business policy is the stable core.
insights.quote: Federal Republicans don’t spend down political capital on cultural issues — they wield them to try to win races.
insights.locator: I think this is a sort of under-discussed
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Blue-state Republicans could be sporadically competitive simply by applying the federal formula to a more left-wing median voter, since every state has business owners and taxpayers and bluer states are more likely to have wasteful spending worth cutting.
insights.so_what: A viable moderate GOP in blue states would act as a check on tax and spending expansion in high-tax states.
insights.quote: the bluer states are in fact more likely to have wasteful spending that’s worth cutting
insights.locator: All you really need to do
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: 1990s precedents show the model works: New York mayor Rudy Giuliani was pro-choice, pro-gay-rights and pro-gun-control, and Los Angeles mayor Richard Riordan had a similar profile, even supporting marriage equality early.
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that socially liberal, fiscally conservative Republicans can win big blue cities.
insights.locator: We used to have a lot of guys like that
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

themes.theme: Trump as the obstacle for blue-state GOP

insights.claim: Donald Trump is a titanic liability for blue-state Republicans because he is super-unpopular there and inserts himself abusively into local affairs, such as efforts to cheat in elections that make voters fear a Republican California governor might subvert midterm House races.
insights.so_what: Trump's national profile caps GOP upside in blue-state races, affecting state-level fiscal and regulatory policy outcomes.
insights.locator: By 2026, I would say blue-state Republicans
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Successful Trump-era blue-state Republicans like former Massachusetts governor Charlie Baker took clear anti-Trump stances, but the Massachusetts GOP went explicitly MAGA after Baker despite no chance of success there.
insights.so_what: State GOP primaries select against electable moderates, reducing competitive two-party checks in blue states.
insights.locator: The successful blue-state Republicans of the Trump era
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: In California's governor race, Republican voters backed Trump supporter Steve Hilton, keeping moderate San Jose mayor Matt Mahan out of the jungle-primary runoff; Hilton now faces Xavier Becerra, who will obviously win, whereas Mahan might have won a runoff against Becerra or Tom Steyer.
insights.so_what: Becerra as California's likely next governor implies continuity of Democratic policy rather than a tough-on-crime, business-friendly reform turn.
insights.quote: Now it’s Hilton in a runoff with Becerra that Becerra is obviously going to win.
insights.locator: Consider the California governor’s race
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Many conservatives seem to prefer watching blue jurisdictions suffer over winning on issues: they are annoyed that Zohran Mamdani's pragmatic policing in New York coincides with falling crime, and many would be happy if California's wealth-tax proposal passes and triggers an economic crisis.
insights.so_what: Flags a live California wealth-tax proposal as a policy risk for high-net-worth residents and the state's economy, with weak organized opposition from the right.
insights.quote: they would enjoy watching the state’s economy suffer a crisis more than they would enjoy getting their way on the issue
insights.locator: This then just raises the question
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Most urban-Northeast Republicans treat land-use regulation as a culture-war topic: New Jersey's Jack Ciattarelli attacked Mikie Sherrill's tepid YIMBY ideas by citing an 'overdevelopment crisis,' and Republicans in New York, Connecticut and Maryland legislatures have been uniformly hostile to zoning reform.
insights.so_what: Bipartisan support for zoning preemption is unlikely in the Northeast, constraining housing supply growth and keeping costs elevated.
insights.locator: Last but not least, most Republicans
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: A pro-business, pro-growth agenda in Northeast states makes no sense while ignoring zoning, which is by far the largest regulatory barrier to growth; NIMBY conservatism there is a crank movement rather than a problem-solving one.
insights.so_what: Land use is framed as the single most important economic issue for states like New York, i.e. the key lever for housing supply and growth.
insights.quote: NIMBY conservatism in the context of the actual urban/suburban American Northeast is just a crank movement rather than a problem-solving one.
insights.locator: I understand the political psychology
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Conservative elites in the Northeast Corridor, including the Manhattan Institute, engage in apologetics rather than plainly saying New York Republicans are on the wrong side of the state's most important economic issue.
insights.so_what: Without elite pressure, state GOP parties are unlikely to pivot toward YIMBY positions.
insights.locator: Unfortunately, I see a lot of conservative elites
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: If an AI research agent hacks a government system on its own, prosecuting the user for an innocuous prompt would be unreasonable; the appropriate response is a negligence case against the LLM maker with financial penalties and ideally a consent decree on model behavior.
insights.so_what: Points to model developers, not users, bearing legal liability for agentic misbehavior — a cost and compliance risk for AI labs.
insights.quote: We’re looking instead at some kind of negligence charge against the maker of the L.L.M.
insights.locator: The genius of common law
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: A big part of the solution to AI-enabled hacking will be AI-enabled cybersecurity, especially because liability deterrents may not work against widely used open-source models.
insights.so_what: Supports demand growth for AI-driven cybersecurity tools as thousands of institutions are forced to harden their defenses.
insights.quote: a big part of the solution to A.I.-enabled hacking is going to be A.I.-enabled cybersecurity
insights.locator: In practice, though
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: Thousands of American institutions that are currently casual about information security will need to tighten practices, including by using AI; this transition will generate grief and dramatic news stories but ultimately land in a fine place.
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of AI-enabled breaches and headlines followed by broad security spending upgrades.
insights.quote: there are currently thousands and thousands of American institutions that can afford to be fairly casual about their information security
insights.locator: Broadly, though, I would say
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: AI hacking is a 'normal technology' problem, like criminals using cars, manageable by common law; the real big AI problems are an intelligence explosion and deceptive alignment leading to genuine loss of human control.
insights.so_what: Distinguishes manageable misuse risks from catastrophic alignment risk, implying regulation should focus on the latter.
insights.quote: the big problems with A.I. are all about the possibility of an intelligence explosion and deceptive alignment leading to a genuine loss of human control
insights.locator: To me, the big problems
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

themes.theme: Coups, legitimacy and the French Revolution counterfactual

insights.claim: The Coup of 18 Fructidor (1797), in which three directors with Talleyrand and Napoleon purged a newly elected monarchist majority, was the key turning point that left a regime with no ideological legitimacy whose only base was the army, making a military dictatorship a logical progression.
insights.so_what: A broader lesson on regime stability: overriding election results to 'save' a system destroys its legitimacy and invites strongman rule.
insights.quote: This was essentially a “destroy the village in order to save it” moment for the French Revolution
insights.locator: What happened here is that the Directory
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias

insights.claim: The 1871 French elections, which produced a divided monarchist majority without a coup and led to the durable Third Republic, suggest that had the 1797 deputies been seated, divided constitutional monarchists might have ended up managing a conservative-leaning republic.
insights.so_what: Illustrates how accepting adverse election results can stabilize democratic institutions over time.
insights.locator: In theory, a monarchist majority
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
